title: Workforce trends shaping hiring in 2027.
summary: Hiring has slowed, but critical roles are still hard to fill. See the workforce trends shaping 2027 hiring and what employers can do about each one.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


- Hiring has slowed, but critical roles are still hard to fill, so plan 2027 headcount role by role and start early on the positions you can't run without.
- Manufacturing demand is outpacing hiring. Recruit from trade programs now and pair new hires with experienced employees before they retire.
- School shortages reach beyond teachers to bus drivers, custodians, and counselors, so plan support-role coverage alongside teaching positions.
- AI is thinning entry-level desk jobs. Keep entry-level roles in the plan and redesign them around mentored, hands-on work.
- Candidate fraud is rising, and pressure to fill roles quickly makes it easier to miss. Verify identity at the start of the hiring process.


A slower U.S. hiring market might make 2027 workforce planning look simpler than it is. With fewer people changing jobs, the experienced candidates employers need most are harder to find. AI is also making it harder to confirm that candidates are who they say they are.


Experience itself is also getting scarcer. Retirements are taking hands-on knowledge out of plants and schools, and AI is reducing the entry-level roles essential for building professional experience.


The five workforce trends below show where hiring will be most challenging in 2027 and what employers can do about each challenge. Across all five, the strongest approach is to plan hiring role by role, starting with the positions your operation can't run without. From there, build the experience those roles require and verify candidates from the start.


## 1. Hiring has slowed, but critical roles are still hard to fill


The U.S. labor market has settled into a low-hire, low-quit pattern, and that pattern makes it challenging to fill critical roles. In September 2026, the


[hires rate was 3.4% and the quits rate was 2.1%](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/jolts.nr0.htm) . When few people change jobs, employers that need the same specialized skills end up recruiting from a small pool.


The long-term outlook points the same way. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects


[total employment to grow just 3.5% from 2025 to 2035](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/ecopro_08272026.htm) , mainly because the population is aging and the labor force is growing more slowly. Executives already see the effect. In the


[Kelly Global Re:work Report](https://www.kellyservices.com/news-insights/2025-rework-report) , 92% of global executives said they're concerned about how retirements will affect labor shortages. Each retirement takes years of hands-on experience out of the workforce, and a slow hiring market won't replace that experience quickly.


A quiet market can make it tempting to put hiring plans on hold, but specialized talent stays scarce even when overall hiring slows. For the roles that keep operations running, waiting means competing for the same small pool later. When a cell therapy manufacturer needed to staff new production suites in


[one of the most competitive markets for that talent](https://set.kellyservices.us/resource-center/business-resources/science/finding-in-demand-scientific-talent-in-a-competitive-market) , Kelly started recruiting right away and brought in 14 experienced specialists in two months.


**What this means for 2027.** Build the headcount plan role by role. Start recruiting early for the positions your operation can't run without, and line up flexible staffing capacity for roles with uneven demand.


## 2. Industrial demand is outrunning hiring


In manufacturing, the open market won't supply enough experienced workers in 2027, so employers will need to build that experience themselves.


**Demand is growing faster than hiring.** Manufacturing job openings reached


[584,000 in September 2026, up from 389,000 a year earlier](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/jolts.nr0.htm) , while the industry's hires rate was 2.5%, below the 3.4% rate across all industries. That means positions stay open longer, and current teams absorb the extra work.


**New talent is heading toward the trades.** In spring 2026, enrollment at vocationally focused community colleges kept growing, while


[computer and information sciences enrollment fell 8.4% at four-year schools](https://nscresearchcenter.org/enrollment-insights/) . More students are preparing for hands-on technical work, which gives manufacturers a growing source of entry-level hires.


**Experience is the hardest part to replace.** In the


[Kelly Global Re:work Report](https://www.kellyservices.com/news-insights/2025-rework-report) , 67% of business professional and industrial executives said they're prepared to keep running as baby boomers retire, but only 55% of their workers agreed. Much of what experienced employees know about equipment, processes, and safety was never written down, and employers need a plan to


[preserve that knowledge](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-to-preserve-institutional-knowledge-before-it-walks-out-the-door) before those employees leave.


**What this means for 2027.** Start recruiting from trade and technical programs now, and pair each new hire with an experienced employee who has time to teach before retiring. Kelly uses a


[hire-train-deploy model](https://www.kellyservices.com/divisions/professional-industrial/expertise/semiconductor) to build that kind of experience in semiconductor manufacturing, growing one client's technician teams from 50 workers to more than 1,400.


## 3. Schools are short-staffed beyond the classroom


School staffing shortages haven't eased, and they reach well past the teaching roles that get most of the attention. About


[1 in 8 teaching positions in the U.S.](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/state-teacher-shortages-2026-factsheet) is either vacant or filled by a teacher who isn't fully certified for the role. In those classrooms, students can end up with more substitutes, larger classes, and less consistent instruction.


The other roles that keep a school running day to day are under similar pressure. The most recent national data shows several of them remain well short of what schools need.


- Custodial staff, where employment is


[12.4% below 2019 levels](https://www.epi.org/blog/the-school-bus-driver-shortage-has-improved-slightly-but-continues-to-stress-k-12-public-education/) .


- Bus drivers, where employment is 9.5% below 2019 levels despite recent wage increases.


- School counselors, at


[about 370 students per counselor](https://www.schoolcounselor.org/getmedia/62807f33-a020-4c4f-ac6f-bf284803fd97/pr_ratios-24-25.pdf) nationally, well above the recommended 250.


These roles get less attention than teaching vacancies, but the school day depends on them. When routes go uncovered or support roles stay open, more work falls to teachers and administrators who already have full schedules.


**What this means for 2027.** Plan coverage for transportation and other support roles alongside teaching positions, and start well before the school year begins.


[Kelly Education](https://www.kellyservices.com/divisions/education/) , the nation's largest provider of education talent, works with more than 10,000 schools to help districts fill those roles.


## 4. AI is shrinking the first rung of desk jobs


AI is cutting into the entry-level desk jobs where people have long learned their professions, and employers that cut those roles now could face an experience shortage later.


### Where entry-level hiring is falling


The decline is concentrated among the youngest workers in the jobs most exposed to AI. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations is


[about 19% below the pace of similar workers in less-exposed jobs](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/news/canariesaug26/) , and that difference has grown over the past year. Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable decline, and the researchers trace the change mainly to reduced hiring. They note the data can't yet prove AI caused it, but the pattern has held since late 2022.


Each entry-level role an employer doesn't fill today is one fewer experienced worker ready to step up in five years.


### Redesign entry-level roles around experience


The work AI absorbs most easily is textbook knowledge, so entry-level roles hold their value when they're built around judgment people learn on the job. The same Stanford research found declines concentrated in roles built on codified knowledge, while employment grew for experienced workers whose roles depend on knowledge gained through practice and mentorship.


AI can also free up the time that kind of learning requires. In the


[Kelly Global Re:work Report](https://www.kellyservices.com/news-insights/2025-rework-report) , 70% of executives said AI should free up time for collaboration, mentoring, or sharing knowledge, but only 47% of workers said they're getting that time back. Directing some of those time savings toward coaching junior employees turns an efficiency gain into a training pipeline.


**What this means for 2027.** Keep entry-level roles in the hiring plan, and redesign them around hands-on, mentored work that builds judgment. Set aside time from AI efficiency gains for experienced employees to coach new hires, and connect that coaching to


[clear learning paths](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-to-upskill-your-employees) .


## 5. Candidate fraud is changing how employers screen


[AI has made it easier for candidates to misrepresent who they are](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-to-spot-fake-job-candidates-before-they-reach-your-payroll) , and the pressure to fill critical roles quickly makes that fraud harder to catch.


In a September 2026 survey of hiring managers by background check provider Checkr,


[40% said they had interviewed a candidate later revealed to be using a fake identity](https://checkr.com/resources/articles/hiring-hoax-manager-survey-2026) , up from 31% a year earlier. The same survey found that 28% of managers had moved a candidate forward despite suspecting dishonesty because the role needed to be filled quickly.


Most AI use by job seekers is legitimate, but it still changes how employers need to screen. In a


[Kelly survey](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/dishonest-job-search-survey-results) , 79% of job seekers said they use AI in their applications, and that volume makes it harder for screeners to spot the candidates using AI to deceive. Timing adds to the risk. Only 29% of companies verify identity when someone applies, so a candidate using a proxy or a fake identity can clear several rounds before anyone checks.


A few changes make fraud easier to catch.


- Verify identity at the application stage, before interviews begin.


- Add a live or in-person step for roles with access to sensitive systems or data.


- Train recruiters and hiring managers to recognize proxy interviews and deepfakes.


- Keep a person reviewing candidates alongside any AI screening tools.


**What this means for 2027.** Protect verification steps for the critical roles you're under the most pressure to fill, since those are where fraud slips through most easily. A staffing partner that vets candidates before they reach your team can take on much of that screening.


## Plan your 2027 hiring with Kelly


A slow hiring market won't make critical roles easier to fill in 2027, and the experience those roles depend on is getting harder to replace. Employers can get ahead of both with three moves. Rank roles by how critical they are and how long they take to fill, then start recruiting for the hardest ones first. Build experience on purpose by recruiting from trade and technical programs, keeping entry-level roles in the plan, and giving experienced employees time to coach. Verify candidates at the start of the process, especially for the roles you're under the most pressure to fill.
